paragraphs.heading: The age we live in
paragraphs.text: The modern era is the period of history we are living in now. The label was first used for Europe and the West, for the time after classical antiquity and the Middle Ages, often counted from around 1500. Since the 1990s, historians have more often called the stretch from the end of the Middle Ages up to the 19th century the early modern period. Today modern is more often kept for the 19th century onward, and the years since the end of World War II in 1945 can also be called contemporary history.

paragraphs.heading: Naming the period
paragraphs.text: The word modern was coined shortly before 1585 to mark the start of a new era. It was long believed that early modern was invented in the 1930s or the mid-20th century, but Justus Nipperdey has pointed out that American historians were already using it widely around 1900. The line between early modern and modern was drawn by the French Revolution and the Industrial Revolution. The European Renaissance, which began in Italy and ran from the 14th to the 16th century, is an important bridge from the late Middle Ages into early modern times.

paragraphs.heading: Early milestones
paragraphs.text: Several events help mark the opening of the period. Johannes Gutenberg's movable-type printing press of the 1450s opened the way to an information age and to newspapers. Columbus's first voyage to the Americas in 1492 began lasting contact between Europe and the New World. Martin Luther's 95 Theses of 1517 set off the Reformation, and in 1543 Copernicus proposed that the Earth goes around the Sun. In 1610 Galileo's Starry Messenger was the first book to publish what someone saw through a telescope.

paragraphs.heading: What changed
paragraphs.text: The modern period brought large developments in science, politics, warfare and technology, and it was also an age of discovery and globalization. European powers, and later their colonies, tightened their political, economic and cultural hold on the rest of the world. The era is closely tied to individualism, capitalism, socialism, the growth of cities, and a belief that technology and politics could keep making things better. It created a new way of living and changed for good how people around the world live.

paragraphs.heading: Old orders replaced
paragraphs.text: Beginning in Western countries, the modern world rethought old value systems, rule by monarchs, and feudal economies. These were often replaced by democratic and liberal ideas in politics, science, psychology, sociology and economics. During the 19th and early 20th centuries, modernist culture, art, science and politics came to dominate not just Western Europe and North America but nearly every part of the globe. That reach included even movements that were thought of as standing against the West and globalization.

paragraphs.heading: Pushback against progress
paragraphs.text: The era also stirred up resistance. The world wars, the Cold War and other conflicts of the era, many of them rooted in fast change, together with the weakening of traditional religious and moral rules, set off many reactions against modern development. More recently, postmodernism has criticised the optimism and faith in constant progress. Postcolonial theory, for its part, has attacked the power that Western Europe and North America held over everyone else.
